cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: When Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933, over 6 million Germans were unemployed - nearly 30% of the workforce. By 1939, official unemployment was under 500,000. The Nazis claimed to have solved the unemployment crisis, but the reality was more complex.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: The Nazis launched massive public works programmes, most famously the autobahn (motorway) network. Between 1933 and 1938, over 3,000 km of autobahn were built. However, the autobahn programme was originally proposed by the Weimar government - the Nazis simply took credit for it.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: Rearmament was the single biggest factor in reducing unemployment. Government spending on arms rose from 3.5 billion marks in 1933 to 30 billion marks by 1939. By 1939, 40% of government expenditure was on the military.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: The National Labour Service (RAD) was made compulsory for all men aged 18-25 in June 1935. They had to serve 6 months doing manual labour - building roads, draining marshes, planting forests, and working on farms. They wore military-style uniforms and lived in camps.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: The Kraft durch Freude (KdF) programme was set up in November 1933 as part of the German Labour Front (DAF). It provided leisure activities for workers - cruises, holidays, trips to the theatre, and sport. By 1938, over 10 million people had taken KdF holidays.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: The Beauty of Labour division of the DAF was established in 1934 to improve working conditions. It pressured employers to provide better facilities: washrooms, canteens, rest areas, and sports facilities. Between 1936-1939, it claimed to have improved 60,000 workplaces.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Nazi Economic Policies
cards.back: Real wages (adjusted for inflation) were only slightly higher in 1939 than in 1928 - and in some industries, they were lower. Workers also lost basic rights: they could not strike, could not change jobs without government permission (labour books from 1935), and had no independent representation. The German Labour Front (DAF) was a state organisation, not a workers' union.

cards.front: What should you know about history exam tips — nazi economic policies?
cards.back: 1. For Nazi Economic Policies, include specific factual detail: dates, names, events and statistics where relevant 2. For source questions, analyse provenance (who, when, why, audience) before using the content 3. In evaluation questions, discuss multiple factors and weigh their relative significance 4. Always link back to the question focus — don't just narrate what happened with Nazi Economic Policies 5. Use phrases like 'the most significant factor was... because...' to show analytical judgement
Autobahns, housing, public buildings (e.g. Created thousands of jobs directly and in supply industries)
Conscription (1935), arms industry expansion (e.g. Removed young men from the workforce; created factory jobs)

cards.front: What does National Labour Service (RAD) mean?
cards.back: Compulsory 6-month service for young men (e.g. Removed thousands from unemployment figures)

cards.front: What does Reintroduction of conscription mean?
cards.back: March 1935; army expanded from 100,000 to 1.4 million by 1939 (e.g. Removed hundreds of thousands from the job market)
Subsidised cruise holidays to Norway, Italy, and Madeira; prices as low as 62 marks for a week's cruise. In 1938, 180,000 went on KdF cruises
Package holidays within Germany; walking trips and ski trips at affordable prices
